title: How many feelings?
hookLine: two, three, five, six, eighteen, a hundred and eight: each count is a way of teaching

lines: A CARPENTER AND A MONK, STUCK.
cards: Two friends are arguing over how many seasons a year has. One says four: spring, summer, fall, winter. The other grew up where the year runs wet, then dry, and says two.
Nobody is lying. They're counting the same year for different reasons. A carpenter named Pancakanga and a monk named Udayi once got stuck in exactly this kind of argument, about feelings.
Neither would budge, and each was quoting the Buddha.

teach.h: THREE FEELINGS, SAYS UDAYI; TWO, SAYS HE
teach.b: This is the fifty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, on many kinds of feeling. Pancakanga, a royal carpenter, asks the monk Udayi: how many feelings did the Buddha teach?
Three, says Udayi: pleasant, painful and neither. No, says Pancakanga, two: pleasant and painful. The neutral one, he says, the Buddha counts as a refined kind of pleasure.
Three. Two. Ananda overhears and tells the Buddha.
Udayi's way was correct, the Buddha says, and Pancakanga didn't accept it. Pancakanga's way was correct, and Udayi didn't accept it.

teach.h: TWO, THREE, FIVE ... A HUNDRED AND EIGHT
teach.b: I've taught two kinds of feeling in one way, three in another, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, and a hundred and eight. Each count is a way of teaching, a lens for a purpose. Then the warning.
When people don't accept what has been well said in another way, you can expect them to quarrel and wound each other with verbal daggers.

When they do accept it, you can expect them to live together like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. You've met both pictures on this path: the daggers of Kosambi and the friends in the Gosinga wood.
Here they meet. The discourse goes on to a ladder of happiness, from the pleasure of the senses to the quieter joys of meditation, each finer than the one before.
Two people can be right about the same thing and still fight, because they're counting differently. Ask what someone is counting for before deciding they're wrong.

how: Some Buddhist teachers point to MN 59 to explain why the scriptures list things in different numbers (two, three or a hundred and eight kinds of feeling) and to encourage harmony when people describe the teaching in different ways.

o: an emotion like anger, joy or fear
a thought about what is happening

games.q: who counted what — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha said Udayi was right and Pancakanga wrong
he said both ways were correct; each simply didn't accept the other's.
the Buddha taught feelings in counts as high as a hundred and eight
two, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, a hundred and eight: each a way of teaching.
the neutral feeling disappears in Pancakanga's count
he counts it as a refined kind of pleasure, within the two.

games.q: two of your students argue: one says you taught three kinds of feeling, the other says two. both have heard you say it. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
o: the one who said three is right.
both are correct; I've taught it many ways.
games.why: the Buddha says both were correct, lists many counts, and warns that refusing another's well-spoken way leads to verbal daggers.

practice: Notice what you feel right now and count it Udayi's way: pleasant, painful, or neither?

Then count it Pancakanga's way, only pleasant or painful, and see where the neutral feeling goes, and how the same moment looks a little different through each lens. Neither is wrong; let counting go, and just feel.

wordCard.voice: Vedana. Feeling: counted two ways, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, a hundred and eight, each true for its purpose.

orig.note: Pali vedana: feeling, the pleasant, painful or neither tone of experience.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways to count. Two people can both be right and still need kind eyes. Day four hundred fifty-one, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 59, Bahuvedaniya Sutta (the many kinds of feeling)
